coder_notes: This is an unambiguous augment-then-split case and the precedence rule applies. The order in the text is explicit: source images are gathered, Matlab augmentation expands them to 10,295, manual screening and 100 negatives bring the final dataset to 10,135, and only then is 'The dataset ... randomly divided into training, validation, and test sets in a 7:2:1 ratio'. The paper's own observation that 'without data augmentation, the model performs well on the training set but poorly on the test set' is consistent with augmented copies propping up the test score. Only the 7:2:1 ratio is given, never the three counts. Nighttime images are stated to be in the dataset but no night-specific result is reported, so night_or_lowlight_tested is no. coder_notes: This is the paper the brief flags as the round-1 over-escalation, and I did not escalate. The two augmentation sentences are 'we applied data augmentation by flipping the data to increase the sample size. The dataset was divided as follows: 80% to train and 20% to test our network.' and, in Implementation Details, 'data augmentation by flipping was exploited for training.' The second locates flipping on the training side; the ordering in the first is genuinely ambiguous, so augment_then_split is not warranted and the code is the ratio-only case. Leakage risk is a close call: the corpus is 46 ERA videos of 150 frames each plus 2003 FLAME pile-burn frames, and the model consumes frame triplets (F(n-2), F(n), F(n+2)), so a frame-level 80/20 would put near-identical neighbours on both sides. The paper never states the mechanism and never claims video-disjointness, so I coded medium rather than high; if the split is frame-level random it would be high. cross_dataset_delta is coded not_reported because the paper states both numbers but never states a drop: in-domain accuracy 0.979 and IoU 0.868 versus Corsican accuracy 94.89 and IoU 0.848, i.e. about 3.0 accuracy points and 2.0 IoU points, computed by me and not by the authors. Fog robustness is tested with algorithmically generated fog, not real weather.

Task coded classification because the reported quantity is image-level fire/non-fire accuracy over two classes, even though the architectures used are detectors (YOLOv8, Detectron2). Several numbers in the paper contradict one another and I did not reconcile them: YOLOv8l is reported at 91.7% train / 90.7% test, the aggregated model at 96.7% train / 97% test (test above train), and recall is given both as 3% ('average precision and recall rate of 97% and 3%') and as 96.1%; recall is also defined incorrectly in the text as 'the ratio of false positives to true positives'. Deployment is also self-contradictory: the model 'was implemented in Raspberry Pi 3B+ to run on GPU mode' while the limitations state 'the current approach's incompatibility with edge devices presents a drawback'. I coded L1 on the implementation statement and flag the contradiction.

coder_notes: Best-documented split in the set, and the only paper that uses the word leakage about itself. The partition is chronological (earlier frames train, later frames validate), which is group_disjoint by time. leakage_risk is the hard call: the rubric's low clause (disjoint by time) and its high clause (same site/event both sides) both literally apply, and the paper itself states that both sides come from one continuous flight over one prescribed pile burn with approximately constant scene, weather and illumination. I coded high on the explicit same-event clause rather than on any inference, and note that the authors are transparent about it rather than concealing it; a coder weighting the time clause would defensibly code low. Two further validity points: there is no held-out test set at all, only a validation split, and the reported checkpoint is 'the checkpoint with the highest validation mAP', i.e. model selection and reporting happen on the same 401 frames. The energy figures are modelled from literature and an LTE UE power model, never measured on flight hardware, so power_measured = estimated. The validity finding here is that none of the rubric's metrics are reported at all: the only quantitative validation is agreement with the existing 3.8 micrometre product ('more than 97% of fire pixels ... passed the accuracy test'), i.e. a comparison against another algorithm's output rather than against ground truth, so there is no precision, recall or false-alarm rate. real_wildfire_detected is yes because the method is run on scenes of actual unplanned wildfires including the 2019-2020 eastern Australia megafire, but this is retrospective processing of archived scenes, not an operational deployment, hence L0; the L0-L5 ladder fits satellite retrospective studies poorly. hyperparams_full is yes in the sense that every threshold constant of the algorithm is stated (R3_cth, T24_cth, k, T24_fth, window growth rule).

coder_notes: split_protocol coded official_heldout because the paper defers to the partition of the dataset paper: 'To ensure experimental consistency, we follow the data partitioning way proposed in [19]', with counts matching 8:1:1 of 2603. The wording 'partitioning way' is the weak point - it could mean re-applying the same 8:1:1 ratio rather than reusing the identical file assignment - so a coder who reads it that way would land on ratio_only_mechanism_unstated instead; I flag it rather than hide it. Leakage risk stays medium because the underlying 2603 images are 'collected from various online sources' with no provenance given and the mechanism inside [19] is not restated here. I did not escalate on augmentation: MixUp at 0.2, copy-paste at 0.3 and scaling at 0.7 are YOLO's on-the-fly training-time pipeline, applied after the partition, and their strength is halved during post-pruning fine-tuning - correct practice. night and haze are coded yes because the results section reports per-scenario outcomes for a low-light row and a hazy row, not merely a claim about dataset composition. seed_reported is yes on the statement that a fixed random seed was used, though the seed value itself is not given. Among the rubric's metrics only mAP is reported; FPS, params and FLOPs are the paper's other three, and the 241 FPS figure is on a CUDA GPU, never on an edge device.
